messages.author: 5e9b9dcf8207ab99
messages.subject: Unidentified model
parts:
I am trying to fit a model on a sample of 200 respondents (no missing data) with twelve interval variables. According to some theory, the most basic form of the model is the following:

#Latent variable definitions
A =~ M + Sg + Mp + Ex
P =~ Self + L + Soc1 + Soc2 + Psy
I =~ MI + T + P

Actually, our hypothesis is the following. The sample can be divided into three groups (by means of a thirteenth categorical variable) and we believe that the above model does not fit well all three groups. Running the above model on the whole sample gave an identified model with poor fit. Running it on Group 2 and Group 3 gave a better fit which, with some modifications, eventually resulted in a model which gave quite a reasonable fit for both Groups 2 and Groups 3.

However, trying to fit the above model to Group 1 gave the following response from lavann (using sem):

Warning messages:
1: In estimateVCOV(lavaanModel, samplestats = lavaanSampleStats, options = lavaanOptions,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not compute standard errors!

2: In lavaan(model = basic, data = monoRecoded.Rdata, model.type = "sem",  :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated variances are negative
3: In lavaan(model = basic, data = monoRecoded.Rdata, model.type = "sem",  :
  lavaan WARNING: residual covariance matrix is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"cov.ov") to investigate.

Now, we were expecting that the basic model would not lead to a good fit for Group 1, but not that it would not be identified. I tried to test Group 1 for multicollinearity. I regressed every one of the twelve observed variables on the others and checked R^2 and the vif, but these gave no indication of multicollinearity. I also checked the covariance matrix for ill-scaling, but there was no evidence of this any more than for Groups 2 and 3.

Incidentally, we tried a different hypothesised model for Group 1 and, again with a few modifications, we finished up with this model which gave an even better fit than the first model for Groups 2 and 3.

#Latent variable definitions
A =~ M + Sg + Ex + Soc1 + Psy
I =~ MI + T + P 

#Covariances
Soc1 ~~ Psy
M ~~ T


This model is approximately in agreement with our initial hypotheses for these groups, so that is ok. But my problem still remains: why is it that the first model could not even be identified for Group 1.

Thanks for any ideas.

Josef

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Unidentified model
parts:
It is possible that the model is just a really bad fit for a constrained factor model, offering no best set of parameter estimates that conforms to rules such as "residual variances must be positive."  One can create a covariance matrix that forces residual variances to be negative without inducing an identification problem.  Look at the parameter estimates that lavaan can provide--see if they are headed off into extreme parameter space.  Also, try looking at the *correlation* matrix only for this group to see if proportionality constraints appear to hold, and if plausible loading values would make sense.
     Also, if there is an identification problem here, it is an empirical identification problem, meaing that it is a problem with the sample data, not the structure of the model per se.  With n = 200 divided into 3 groups, the membership in Group 1 may be fairly small, so that the algorithm does not detect some effects as significant because of low n, leading in turn to an identification problem.
     Remember that, with an iterative estimation procedure, empirical identification is a matter of the parameter estimates right now, on this iteration.  Sometimes estimation runs temporarily through bad parameter space, but it could come out into good estimates if it had the chance.  You could try to avoid the bad parameter space by setting starting values that are "different from zero" and on the same side of zero where you expect the final estimates to fall.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 5e9b9dcf8207ab99
messages.subject: Re: Unidentified model
parts:
Thanks Edward! 

Yes, it must be an empirical identification problem (see more below). Size for the problem Group 1 is 64 while for the other two groups sizes are 96 and 40. We are trying to get a larger sample, but depends on research funds! I'll try out what you said. 

Question: What do you mean by "proportionality constraints" in the correlation matrix? I did calculate the correlation matrix for the group but did not see any unduly large values. 

To put you in better picture: I tried out the first simple model for all the sample with poor fit. I then did the same with "groups=categorical_variable" and I got the error message which I posted for Group 1. At that point I was forced to consider Group 1 and Groups 2 & 3 separately. Strangely, when I got the final two models (Model 1 with reasonable fit for Group 1 and Model 2 with reasonable fit for Groups 2 and 3) Model 2 applied to Group 1 still gave me the same sort of error as the one I had posted, while Model 1 for the other two groups was ok for the group of size 40 but again gave me those errors for the group of size 96. So yes, it must be something related to data, but not immediately related to size, it seems.

Thanks.

Josef

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Unidentified model
parts:
Josef--
     A chapter by Karl Joreskog, "Basic Ideas in Factor and Component Analysis" first explained this to me.
     If two observed variables A and B are both congeneric indicators of the same single common factor, then the ratio of their correlations with any third variable C must be a constant ratio or proportion across all other C in the model, at the population level.  So at the population level is must be true that:
corr(A,C) / corr(B,C) is a constant across all C.
    So you can look at a correlation matrix and determine whether a given factor model seems to hold, without estimating a model.  You can at least see gross violations of these proportionality constraints.  Your n is low, so there will be a lot of random sampling error obscuring the correlations, but you might be able to visually detect the kind of major reversal of proportionality, such as (for any two other variables C and D):
corr(A,C) > corr(B,C) but  corr(A,D) < corr(B,D) 
which would signal a major fit problem.
     So what I was asking was whether the correlation matrix looked like the factor model ought to hold.  If you saw a major problem, that could explain a failure to converge normally, even if the moel isn technically identified.
--Ed Rigdon
